title: Every Ruler Who Built This Fort Is on the Record. Its Most Famous Defender Isn't.
standfirst: Chitradurga Fort was raised over two centuries by a line of tax-funded chieftains whose reigns, assassinations and betrayals are documented in some detail. The soldier's wife credited with holding off Hyder Ali's men with a wooden pestle appears in no record from either side — and Karnataka made her a public holiday anyway.

sections.heading: Every Ruler Here Left a Paper Trail. She Didn't.
sections.body:
In 1779, on Hyder Ali's third attempt to take the fort, his soldiers found a gap in the outer rock wall and began pushing men through it after dark. The guard posted at that stretch, Kahale Mudda Hanuma, had gone home for his midday meal; his wife, Onake Obavva, walked to a nearby pond for water and saw the soldiers coming through the hole. She killed them one at a time with the onake — the long wooden pestle she had carried to fetch water — dragging each body aside before the next man climbed through, so the column behind him suspected nothing. She was found dead later that same day; some tellings say from shock, others say an enemy blade reached her first.

No court record from the Chitradurga Nayakas' own administration mentions her. Neither do Hyder Ali's military papers, nor anything the East India Company was writing about the region in that decade. The story survives because it was carried in Kannada ballads for more than a century before anyone wrote it down. None of that has stopped the state acting on it: Karnataka has marked 11 November as [Onake Obavva Jayanti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onake_Obavva) since 2021, a statue of her stands outside the Chitradurga district commissioner's office, and a stadium carries her name.

sections.heading: Seven Walls Raised by a Chain of Tax-Collecting Chieftains, Not One Architect
sections.body:
Fortification of the outcrop above modern Chitradurga began under the Chalukyas and Hoysalas sometime in the 11th to 13th centuries, before any Nayaka ruled here. What turned it into the fort in the photograph above came after the Vijayanagara Empire took the region from the Hoysalas and installed local chieftains to govern it as feudatories. The first named among them, Timmanna Nayaka of Matti, governed the Davangere and Chitradurga districts on Vijayanagara's behalf and died around 1588 a prisoner of the empire he served — broadly the same fate that would end the dynasty two centuries later. His son, later known as Madakari Nayaka I, took over that year and ruled until 1602.

What the family built afterward was less a single design than an accumulation, funded out of tax revenue rather than one commission. The [seven concentric walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chitradurga_Fort) — Elusuttina Kote in Kannada, ["fort of seven circles"](https://30stades.com/travel/chitradurga-fort-with-legends-military-architecture-rainwater-harvesting-karanataka-8769690) — eventually ran about 8 kilometres, enclosing roughly 1,500 acres, with walls between 5 and 13 metres high, pierced by 19 main gateways, 38 postern gates, 35 secret entrances and four passages built to be invisible. In the oldest stretches the granite blocks are cut and fitted with no mortar at all; later work switches to fired brick set in mortar, a change that marks new money and new masons more than any single plan.

sections.heading: Two Rulers Assassinated by Their Own Chiefs Within Three Years
sections.body:
The money behind all that stonework was substantial by regional standards: under Kasturi Rangappa Nayaka I, who ruled from 1602 to 1652, the principality's revenue reportedly reached around 65,000 Durgi pagodas a year by the end of his reign. The throne that revenue paid for was not correspondingly secure. Obanna Nayaka II, who took power in 1674, was assassinated by his own chiefs within the year; his successor, Shoora Kantha Nayaka, met the same fate in 1676. Nothing in the [surviving record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nayakas_of_Chitradurga) names the assassins or explains their motive — only that, twice within three years, the men closest to power removed the man holding it.

Bharamappa Nayaka, who ruled from 1689 to 1721, is the one later ruler for whom specific building work survives in the record by name: after allying with the Marathas at the Battle of Dodderi in 1695 and earning the epithet Bichchugatti Bahramanna Nayaka, he funded temples and irrigation works, among them the Ranganatha Swamy temple at Niratadi. Set against a reign of thirty-two years, that is not a long list — which says less about what Bharamappa actually built than about how little of any Nayaka's building programme made it into writing at all.

sections.heading: He Beat Hyder Ali Twice. The Third Time, His Allies Sold Him Out.
sections.body:
By the time [Madakari Nayaka V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madakari_Nayaka_V) succeeded in 1758, Chitradurga sat in the middle of a fight it had little real chance of staying out of: the Maratha Empire and the rapidly expanding Kingdom of Mysore, under Hyder Ali, both wanted control of central Karnataka, and Madakari spent his reign playing one against the other — negotiating with the Marathas for protection while, at other times, cooperating with Hyder Ali directly. The strategy bought the fort two outright wins. Hyder Ali attacked in 1760 and again in 1770, and both times the fort held: its cascading reservoirs stored enough rainwater to outlast a siege, and its granaries were built to feed a garrison through one.

The third attempt, in 1779, succeeded. Madakari's gamble on both sides at once finally failed him — he was betrayed by his Maratha allies and by some of his own officers, and the fort fell after roughly two centuries of Nayaka rule.

sections.heading: Wikipedia's Own Pages Don't Agree on How the Last Nayaka Died
sections.body:
What happened to Madakari after 1779 is not settled even in the sources that exist. The Wikipedia article on the fort itself states that he was ["taken prisoner and killed"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chitradurga_Fort). The separate article on Madakari Nayaka V, and the article on the Nayakas of Chitradurga as a dynasty, both instead say only that he [died in captivity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madakari_Nayaka_V) at Srirangapatna, where Hyder Ali held him along with members of his family — a version that leaves open whether his death was an execution or simply an imprisonment he did not survive. Bedar soldiers and families from Chitradurga were moved to Srirangapatna too, many absorbed into the Mysore army that had just defeated them.

The fort itself kept working for other people. Hyder Ali's son Tipu Sultan used the lower fort as an [administrative outpost](https://30stades.com/travel/chitradurga-fort-with-legends-military-architecture-rainwater-harvesting-karanataka-8769690) and installed a mill there for grinding gunpowder. After Tipu was killed fighting the British in 1799, British troops garrisoned Chitradurga themselves until 1809, when they handed it back to the government of Mysore. The Archaeological Survey of India protects it now, open from dawn to dusk. Every ruler who taxed the land to build this fort is on the record somewhere, however incompletely — a name, a reign, a manner of death disputed by one sentence against another. Obavva, who has none of that, is the one Karnataka still gives a public holiday to.
